transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-08
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Samantha (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Priya (CTO), Mark (InfoSec), Jules (Platform)

Summary:
Short review of Redwood audit logs and admin activity capabilities: what events are captured (admin actions, role changes, API keys, model rollouts), export options (S3/CSV/syslog), retention policy flexibility, and encryption/KMS integration. Customer (Argent Bank) has strict retention and residency constraints and asked about proof points (SOC 2) and ability to stream logs into their SIEM.

Topics:
- What audit events are captured and their fidelity
- Export and streaming options (S3, syslog, webhook)
- Retention policy and legal hold / e-discovery
- RBAC / admin role events and SSO provisioning logs
- Encryption and KMS/HSM integration
- Demo of export flow and sample log schema (high level)

Action items (recorded in meeting): see metadata for owners/due dates

Transcript:
00:00 Samantha: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Samantha from Redwood. Diego from our SE team will cover the audit depth and export options. How are you all doing?
00:10 Priya: Good thanks, short on time so we'll go through compliance items first. Mark is leading the questions.
00:18 Mark: Yeah we mostly care about admin activity logging, retention, and proving tamper-evidence for audits. Also SIEM integration.
00:28 Diego: Great, that's what we're focused on today. Quick note, I might mangle some product names — transcription sometimes reads KV cash instead of KV cache — sorry in advance.
00:36 Samantha: Quick background—Argent's production will be multi-region, some workloads on-prem. We did a quick intake form: key asks were SOC two, RBAC events, SSO provisioning logs, export to S3 or our Azure blob, and integration with our KMS.
00:52 Priya: Correct. We also need admin actions tied to identity (who made change, from where). The logs need to include request IDs and request bodies where appropriate for forensic.
01:05 Diego: On the Redwood side we capture a pretty broad set: authentication events (SSO/SAML logins, token creations), admin console actions (role changes, user invites, policy changes), API key creation/revocation, model rollout operations, config changes, and export/ingest events. Each event includes timestamp, actor identity, IP, request ID, and an action payload when applicable.
01:32 Mark: Do you include the pre/post state for things like role changes? For audits we sometimes need to show previous role membership.
01:40 Diego: We include a delta object in the event for most admin actions — delta may be summarized in the UI and included in the export. The transcript might show that as 'previous' and 'current' fields (export schema) — sometimes the auto-transcription will say 'previous and curry ant' which is nonsense.
01:55 Jules: How big are those events? If we include full request bodies, logs could get large, and we have retention at 7 years for certain records. Storage and cost are a concern.
02:07 Diego: Right, we let customers configure level-of-detail. By default we store metadata + a summarized payload. For customers who need full bodies for legal reasons, we can enable full-verbosity exports. That increases size; we offer lifecycle helpers to tier older logs to colder storage and straight to your S3 with lifecycle rules.
02:25 Mark: Encryption at rest — can you integrate with our KMS/HSM? We need customer-managed keys for exported logs and for the control plane metadata.
02:34 Diego: Yes — Redwood supports envelope encryption with customer-managed keys via AWS KMS or Azure KeyVault. For on-prem we also support HSM integrations; we can provide details in the security whitepaper. Exports to S3 can be server-side encrypted with your KMS key.
02:49 Priya: About streaming to our Splunk or SIEM — do you have a syslog collector or do we poll an S3 bucket?
02:56 Diego: Both patterns are supported. We can push logs in near-real-time to a syslog endpoint or provide structured JSON exports to S3 that you can ingest via your ETL. We also have a webhook-based streaming option for lower-volume events. Latency is typically seconds to a minute depending on throughput.
03:15 Mark: How do you ensure logs are tamper-evident? For audits we prefer append-only with checksums or signatures.
03:22 Diego: We sign batches of logs with an internal HMAC and can provide cryptographic hashes on demand. For enterprise customers we can set up an append-only storage workflow with signed manifests and store manifests in your bucket or a retention vault. We'll add the manifest signature details to the export doc.
03:37 Samantha: Quick clarification — when we say "admin actions" that includes rollout events for model versions, correct?
03:41 Diego: Yes, model rollouts, canary switches, and routing policy changes are tracked as admin events. We record the model id, version, who triggered it, and the previous routing.
03:52 Priya: Good. Also we need SSO provisioning and de-provisioning events from SCIM. Those need to be correlated with our identity provider logs.
04:00 Diego: SCIM provisioning events are included. We record create/update/delete, and we include the SCIM user id and the identity provider id to make correlation easier.
04:10 Jules: For retention — is there an admin UI to set retention windows per event type? We want to keep auth events for 12 months, admin changes for 7 years, and debug traces for 30 days.
04:20 Diego: Yes, retention policies can be configured at the org and event-type level. We provide defaults and you can override. We also support legal holds — if a log is under hold it won't be eligible for automatic deletion.
04:33 Mark: Any limits on retention length? We have some regs that require multiple years.
04:38 Diego: No hard upper limit— retention is configurable; practical limits are cost and storage quotas. For long-term retention we recommend exporting to your long-term S3 bucket and enabling Glacier or vendor-equivalent. Redwood can automate exports on a schedule.
04:54 Priya: About exports — can we schedule a daily full export and also have near-real-time streaming for critical events?
05:00 Diego: Yes, you can do both. Near-real-time for high-priority events (auth failures, admin role changes) and batched full exports for the archive. The streaming uses our streaming pipeline and can be throttled/filtered.
05:12 Mark: For the streaming endpoint, is there an ack mechanism? We want to know if our SIEM accepted the payload.
05:18 Diego: We support at-least-once delivery with retries and a dead-letter queue for failed deliveries. Delivery receipts are provided and can be exported to your SIEM for monitoring.
05:29 Jules: How about cross-region residency? Some logs must stay in EU only.
05:33 Diego: Redwood supports region-bound exports and we can pin exports to a specific region's S3 or blob storage. For private deployments we can ensure logs never leave your VPC. We'll note that in the architecture doc.
05:44 Samantha: Quick pause for any immediate red flags?
05:48 Mark: One ask: we need certified SOC 2 (type II) evidence for the control of logging and retention. Do you have that?
05:54 Samantha: Yes we have SOC 2 type II; we'll share the report under NDA. I'll attach the certificate and our audit-logs section.
06:01 Priya: Great. Also we need to know about admin console RBAC logs — do you capture which UI user clicked what and the originating IP?
06:09 Diego: Yes — UI actions are instrumented; we surface the UI action name, actor id, IP, user-agent, and a request id linking to the server-side event.
06:20 Jules: For PII — are request bodies redacted by default? We need to avoid storing customer PII in logs where possible.
06:28 Diego: By default we redact PII from logs (email addresses, certain sensitive fields). For customers who require full payloads we can turn that off, but we recommend using redaction rules or tokenization. We'll include the redaction policy in the doc.
06:42 Mark: Can we run a short PoC where we send a week of logs into our S3 and validate ingest and retention lifecycle?
06:48 Samantha: Absolutely. Diego can run the export. Jules, can you take the lead from Argent side to coordinate bucket access?
06:54 Jules: Yes I'll set up a test bucket and share credentials; prefer cross-account role rather than access keys.
07:01 Diego: Cross-account role is supported; we'll provide a CloudFormation snippet or Terraform to attach the role with least privileges.
07:10 Priya: Any support for SIEM parsers? We use Splunk — do you provide example props/transforms?
07:17 Diego: We have Splunk ingestion examples and prebuilt sourcetypes that map our JSON schema. We'll share the Splunk props.conf example in the doc.
07:27 Mark: About retention immutability — can we lock a set of logs for a legal hold? We need WORM-like capabilities.
07:34 Diego: We can mark exports with immutability flags if your storage supports it (S3 Object Lock). Redwood can set the object lock headers during export.
07:43 Samantha: All right, let's walk through a quick mock export flow — Diego, can you briefly describe the steps?
07:49 Diego: Sure — step 1: customer provides destination (S3/Blob) and access method (cross-account role or keys); step 2: Redwood creates a daily/export job and streams high-priority events in near-real-time; step 3: each exported file includes a manifest and a cryptographic signature; step 4: lifecycle rules can move older files to Glacier; step 5: retention config is applied at the Redwood side and optionally enforced via object lock.
08:15 Jules: Sounds good. For the manifest signature, do you provide a public key we can verify?
08:20 Diego: Yes we can publish a verification key or provide per-customer certificates. We'll include options in the doc.
08:28 Priya: One last question — for on-prem/private, can the audit logs be kept entirely inside our network?
08:34 Diego: Yes. In Private deployments we can route audit logs to internal storage and disable uplinks to Redwood's hosted buckets. That gives you full control over retention and residency.
08:44 Mark: What about alerting — can you trigger alerts from certain admin events?
08:49 Diego: Yes, we have alerting hooks; you can configure webhooks, email, or pager duty triggers for defined events. Those alerts can also be exported to your SIEM as events.
08:59 Samantha: Cool. We're at about 9 minutes in the transcript log here — note actual call is 45 minutes, this is an excerpted transcript style with timestamps at key points.
09:08 Priya: Ok next steps — we need the SOC 2 report, the export schema, sample manifest signature, and a scheduled PoC export.
09:16 Samantha: I'll send SOC 2 and the audit-logs doc today, Diego will run the export and sample data, Jules will provide bucket/role. We'll aim to have the PoC running early next week.
09:26 Mark: Also include a quick runbook for legal hold and an outline of how to prove tamper-evidence during audit.
09:33 Samantha: Noted. Any other questions?
09:36 Priya: No, that's it for now. Thanks.
09:40 Samantha: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with the docs and a calendar invite for the export run.

Recap (end of call):
- Redwood to share SOC 2 Type II report and audit-logs export documentation (Samantha)
- SE to run sample export and share Splunk configs + manifest signature examples (Diego)
- Customer to provide test bucket/role and retention constraints (Jules/Mark)

Referenced artifacts and links (shared in chat):
- Redwood SOC 2 report (link sent via secure share)
- Audit logs schema doc (redwood.com/secure/audit-logs-schema) [placeholder link]
- Splunk ingestion example (props.conf snippet)
- CloudFormation cross-account role snippet (sent by Diego)

End.
